trick: Statements are the whole world: no outside facts. 'Only A are B' means every B is an A (B sits inside A), nothing more.

Assumption = what the speaker takes for granted; strong argument = direct + important; 'only way' fails.

ex.q:
Three statements are given, followed by four conclusions numbered I to IV. Assuming the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the conclusions logically follow(s) from the given statements.
Statements:
All copies are books.
Some books are magazines.
All magazines are newspapers.
Conclusions:
I. Some magazines are copies.
II. Some magazines are books.
III. Some newspapers are magazines.
IV. No magazine is copy.
o: Only conclusion I and III follow.
Either conclusion I or IV follows.
Conclusion II and either I or IV follows.
Conclusion II and III and either I or IV follows.
steps: Basic diagram: copies inside books; books overlap magazines; magazines inside newspapers.
II follows (some books are magazines, read in reverse); III follows (all magazines are newspapers).
I, IV: no fixed link between magazines and copies; same terms, Some/No pair, so either I or IV.
Answer: Conclusion II and III and either I or IV follows.

ex.q:
In a certain code language,
A @ B means 'A is the mother of B',
A × B means 'A is the wife of B',
A + B means 'A is the brother of B' and
A ÷ B means 'A is the father of B'.
How is S related to H if 'S × D ÷ R + Y @ H'?
steps: S × D: S(−) is D's wife. D ÷ R: D(+) is R's father. R + Y: R(+) is Y's brother, so Y is D and S's child.
Y @ H: Y(−) is H's mother.
From H's side: mother Y, and Y's mother is S. Answer: Mother's mother.

ex.q: A, B, C, D, E, F and G are sitting around a circular table facing the centre. Only one person sits between G and C when counted from the left of C. E sits third to the right of A. F sits third to the left of D. E sits to the immediate right of F. B is not an immediate neighbour of F. Who sits third to the right of G?
steps: Seats counted to the right: A = 0, E = 3; E is just right of F, so F = 2; F is 3rd left of D, so D = 5.
B, C, G take 1, 4, 6; B is not at 1 (next to F). G is 2nd left of C: C = 1, G = 6, B = 4.
Third to the right of G: 6 + 3 = 9, less 7 = seat 2 = F.

Relative speed: same direction a − b, opposite directions a + b
Boat: still water = (down + up)/2, stream = (down − up)/2
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time; two equal distances: 2ab/(a + b)
Same distance: speed ∝ 1/time; one turns back at the end: together they cover 2D

Past the platform: 63 km/h = 17.5 m/s, 17.5 × 30 = 525 m = train + platform

The following bar graph indicates the demand and production (in hundreds) of 5 companies A, B, C, D and E. X-axis indicates the demand and production (in hundreds) and Y-axis indicates the companies. Study the bar graph carefully and answer the question that follows.

E.per: 2.5 a paper, in all 10 sets (6 in the 8 Oct set)
forms: Indirect to direct, 18 of 25: '... the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Direct Speech.'
Direct to indirect, 7 of 25: 'Choose the correct indirect narration of the following statement ...'
Statements, 14: had started, had been waiting, would have left, a report inside a report, if-clauses
Questions, 5: asked if, asked why, asked whether, wondered whether
Commands and requests, 5: ordered, reminded, requested, asked ... to; 'Please ...'
Exclamation, 1: exclaimed with joy, 'Hurrah! We have won ...'
trick: Tense one step back: V1 → V2, is → was, are → were, has → had, V2 → had + V3, will → would, can → could.
Pronouns: I/we match the speaker, you the listener; this → that, these → those, here → there, come → go.
Time words: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the previous day.
Questions: asked + if/whether (yes/no) or + wh-word, then statement order, no '?': asked me if I was going.
Commands: ordered/asked + object + to + V1 (asked the trainees to go on); 'Please' → requested + to + V1.
No shift: universal truths, a past perfect already there (had made stays), had ... might have if-clauses.
Back to direct (18 of 25): undo every shift; told → said to; requested → 'Please ...'; ordered → bare order.

ex.q:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.
He asked me if I was going to attend the conference the next day.
o: He said to me, "Are you going to attend the conference tomorrow?"
He said to me, "Were you going to attend the conference tomorrow?"
He said to me, "Will you attend the conference the next day?"
He said to me, "Are you going to attend the conference the next day?"
steps: 'asked ... if' is a yes/no question, so the direct form is said to + a question opening with the helping verb.
Undo the shifts: was going → are going, I (the listener) → you, the next day → tomorrow.
B keeps the past 'Were'; C and D keep 'the next day'. Only A undoes all three.

E.per: 2.4 a paper, in all 10 sets (2 or 3 each time)
forms: Select the correctly spelt word, four spellings of one word: 13 of 24

Identify the incorrectly spelt word in the sentence and rectify it: 2
Replace the highlighted word, or 'No replacement required': 1
trick: Build it from parts: un + assail + able, in + dispens + able, un + precedent + ed, play + wright (a maker).
Doubles decide most: accommodation (cc, mm) and reconnaissance (nn, ss), each asked twice; surveillance (ll).
Sounds-like traps: -able not -ible (indispensable), -ance not -ence (surveillance), consensus not concensus.

ex.q: In the following question, four spellings are given. Select the correctly spelt word.
steps: Say it in parts: ac-com-mo-da-tion, double c and double m.
A drops an m, C drops a c, D drops an m and the i.

forms: Active to passive 12, passive to active 10
Continuous: is repairing, was instructing, should be reviewing, were being monitored
Perfect: has approved, has been installed, will have been announced
Modals: might postpone, must be followed, must have made the guests sit
Who-question, twice: Who broke the expensive vase in the living room?
Command: Take a pair of binoculars with you lest ...
Two verbs: ate ... had kept; exclaimed that ...; has prepared ... to serve; is said to have been developed
trick: Object becomes subject, the doer goes after 'by', the tense never changes. Wrong options change the tense.
be + V3 by tense: is/was + V3; is/was being + V3; has/had been + V3; might/must be + V3; must have been + V3.
Who + V2 ...? → By whom + was/were + object + V3? Never 'By who', and the helper comes before the object.
Command → Let + object + be + V3 (Let a pair of binoculars be taken); 'lest' keeps should (should be missed).
Two verbs: each keeps its own tense (ate → was eaten, had kept → had been kept); that-clause → It was ...
Infinitives: to serve → to be served; made the guests sit → were made to sit ('to' comes back).
No doer named: drop 'by them'; going to active, supply They or People (They reserved a table).

ex.q:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.
The tiger ate all the flesh that the zoo-keeper had kept in the enclosure.
o: All the flesh that had been kept by the zoo-keeper in the enclosure was eaten by the tiger.
All the flesh that was kept by the zoo-keeper in the enclosure was eaten by the tiger.
All the flesh that had been kept by the zoo-keeper in the enclosure had been eaten by the tiger.
All the flesh that was kept by the zoo-keeper in the enclosure had been eaten by the tiger.
steps: Two verbs, each keeps its own tense: ate (V2) → was eaten; had kept (had + V3) → had been kept.
B and D lose the past perfect in the that-clause; C and D push 'ate' into the past perfect.

forms: Meaning of the given idiom, 14 of 20: 'Select the most appropriate meaning of the following idiom:'
Meaning of an idiom used in a sentence, 3: head above water, bite the bullet, dark horse
Fill in the blank with the correct expression, 2: fell flat, bite the bullet
Meaning given, pick the idiom, 1: With bells on
trick: Picture the scene, then take its sense: floodgates open = release, a straw in the wind = an early sign.
In a sentence, the sentence decides: 'Despite the challenges, ... head above water' = barely coping.
Traps: the literal picture (a law textbook for the Riot Act) and a look-alike idiom (at the last minute).

From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.
Be up to the minute.
o: At the last possible instant or opportunity
To be as current as is possible
steps: Up to the minute = the very latest, fully current (up-to-the-minute news).
A is the meaning of 'at the last minute', a look-alike idiom: the trap.

forms: Four parts, pick the part with the error: 15 of 19 (three offered 'No error')
Three sentences, 4 (1 Oct): 'Identify which of the given three sentences are grammatically and contextually accurate.'
trick: One of the + plural noun (one of the most difficult problems); one of those officers who + plural verb.
Each of / Neither of + singular verb and his/its (Each of the boys was given a prize for his ...).
Neither ... nor: verb agrees with the nearer subject; along with / as well as / together with: the first.
Hardly / Scarcely ... when; No sooner ... than. These pairs came in 4 questions.
Articles by sound (a unique); no 'a' before applause; never 'most unique'; a party acting as one takes its.
After to / did use V1 (to give, did not go); look forward to + V-ing (to meeting).
Set pairs: not only X but also Y in the same form (no extra 'to'); events take place, not give place.

1. Hardly had he left the room than it started raining heavily.
2. The principal, as well as the teachers, is attending the seminar.
3. Each of the boys were given a prize for their performance.
Identify which of the given three sentences are grammatically and contextually accurate.
steps: 1 is wrong: Hardly pairs with when, not than.
2 is right: with 'as well as' the verb follows the first subject, The principal → is.
3 is wrong: Each of the boys is singular → was given ... his performance.

forms: Single word, 13 of 16: 'Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.'
Word inside a sentence, 2: 'Which word is nearest in meaning to demonstrating?', 'Which word can best replace ingenuity?'

trick: Fix the word's direction (good or bad, more or less): in 9 of 15, two or three options were its opposites.
Word families: zeal → zealous (eager), asper (rough) → asperity (harshness), ex + skin → excoriate (condemn).
Sounds-like traps: zealous is not jealous (Envious was offered), jejune is not juvenile (Young was offered).

Select the most appropriate synonym of the word given below.
Mitigate
steps: Mitigate = make less severe.
Aggravate and intensify make it worse, instigate stirs it up: strike all three.
Alleviate is left. The pair came back on 5 Oct as an antonym: ALLEVIATE → Aggravate.

Same task, other stems: 'Out of the four alternatives, select the word opposite in meaning ...', 'What is the antonym of ...?'
trick: Three options are synonyms of the word: the odd one out is the answer (12 of 14 in 2026).
Prefix cue: im-/in- can mean not (impecunious = moneyless → opulent), yet incipient = beginning (→ mature).
Trap: an option that looks like the word is its synonym, never the answer (Private for Privy).

steps: Impecunious = having no money (im- not + pecunia money).
Destitute, bankrupt and penurious all mean poor: three synonyms, so none is the answer.
The odd one out, opulent (very rich), is the antonym.

E.per: 2.7 a paper, in 8 of 10 sets (4 or 5 in each set since 6 Oct)
forms: Four sentences labelled 1-4, A-D or P-S, pick the order: 21 of 27
S1 fixed, or S1 and S2 fixed with four jumbled between: 3
Parts of one sentence or news report: 3 (6 and 7 Oct)
trick: Opener: names the topic in full, no pronoun, no linker ('Phytoplankton play ...', 'Electric vehicles (EVs)').
Never first: This/These/It/They/Its, 'The technique' (a noun met before), However, Moreover, Therefore.
A pointer follows its noun at once: 'These microscopic organisms' goes straight after the Phytoplankton line.
Linkers: Moreover, In addition add a point; However brings a problem; Therefore, As a result give the result.
Closer: a conclusion (Therefore, As a result, Together, these ...), a remedy, or a final 'However' downside.
Use the options: fix the opener and strike; one pointer pair then decides between what is left.
Fragments: join the part that ends mid-phrase to the one that finishes it (is a forum + of space scientists).

ex.q:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:
1. These microscopic organisms form the base of the marine food web.
2. However, ocean acidification is threatening their survival by dissolving their calcium carbonate shells.
3. Phytoplankton play a crucial role in maintaining the health of our oceans.
4. Without them, the entire marine ecosystem could face a catastrophic collapse.
steps: Opener: 3 names Phytoplankton; 1 (These), 2 (However) and 4 (Without them) cannot open. A or C is left.
'These microscopic organisms' (1) must follow 3 directly: 3, 1. That rules out C.
Check: 2 brings the threat (However), 4 closes with the collapse (Without them).

The digital revolution, for all its emancipatory promise, has spawned a (1)________ of misinformation that threatens the very foundations of informed discourse.

repeats.q: In a certain coded language 'COMPS' is coded as 'NKHKY' and 'ABATE' is coded as 'ZOVXW'. How will 'SMOKY' be coded in the same code language?
repeats.e:
Write the word in reverse, then shift letters back by 5, 5, 5, 4, 4.
COMPS → SPMOC → S−5=N, P−5=K, M−5=H, O−4=K, C−4=Y → NKHKY; ABATE → ETABA → Z, O, V, X, W ✓.
SMOKY → YKOMS → Y−5=T, K−5=F, O−5=J, M−4=I, S−4=O → TFJIO.
Answer: TFJIO

The six boxes form a ring; every symbol moves one place clockwise: top-left → top-middle → top-right → bottom-right → bottom-middle → bottom-left → top-left.
